cover.title: Rebuilding Lebanon’s Fiscal Contract for a Fairer Society
cover.hook: Lebanon’s 2027 draft budget balances at around $7 billion. **Who pays, and who benefits?**

chapters.title: A balanced budget. What does it tell us?

text: Lebanon’s financial collapse changed the size of the state. Public expenditure fell from about **$15.2 billion in 2019** to **$6 billion in 2026**.
The **2027 draft budget**, now before Parliament, would spend **around $7 billion**. All three bars are drawn on the same scale.
On paper, the draft balances. Projected revenue and projected spending both come to **around $7 billion**, a projected deficit of zero.
But a zero deficit leaves the state’s **debt and accumulated liabilities unaddressed**. It also reveals little about who finances the state and who benefits from its spending.
TPI’s research shows that the tax burden has shifted toward lower-income households.
The **poorest half of households**, whose income equals 11% of GDP, paid **20% of all taxes in 2019** and **26% in 2026**.
Over the same period, the share paid by the **richest 1%**, whose income equals 20% of GDP and who hold about one-third of national wealth, fell from **14% to 7%**.
**Consumption taxes account for about 79% of tax revenue.** Income, profits and wealth remain largely untaxed.
The 2027 draft continues this pattern. It projects **total revenue rising by 14.2%**.

**Fuel taxes and VAT account for more than half** of the additional tax revenue. Exemptions are left intact without justification, and revenue targets rest on optimistic assumptions amid a contracting economy.
Public spending traceable to beneficiaries fell from **$13 billion in 2019** to **$4.3 billion in 2026**.
The amount reaching the **poorest half of households**, mostly through public hospitalization and social protection, fell from **$814 million in 2019** to **$617 million in 2026**.
In 2026, **youth and families received only 15%** of traceable spending.

chapters.title: Where does the proposed spending increase go?

text: In the 2027 draft, **personnel costs absorb more than 90%** of the proposed spending increase.
That would bring **personnel costs to 65% of the full budget**.
**Capital spending would rise by only around $25 million**, despite vast reconstruction and infrastructure needs. Resources reaching beneficiaries directly remain limited.

questions.title: What should Lebanon’s budget do over the next five years?
questions.intro: The roundtable shifts the debate from these shortcomings to what the budget should become. It asks four questions.
items: How should Lebanon raise and allocate public resources?
What reforms would make those choices possible?

purpose.title: Why this roundtable
purpose.intro: The roundtable brings together policymakers, public officials and experts to work towards a more equitable, efficient and sustainable fiscal system.

items.title: A shared starting point
items.text: Participants will use TPI’s research on who pays taxes and who benefits from public spending as a common evidence base.

items.title: Concrete options
items.text: They will debate options for taxation, exemptions, spending and public financial management.

items.title: Feasibility and trade-offs
items.text: They will examine the feasibility and trade-offs of reforms, including their effects on vulnerable households.

items.title: What comes next
items.text: Areas of agreement and open questions will inform TPI’s forthcoming report, **“What Should the Budget Be?”**

notes: All figures are taken from TPI’s concept note for the policy roundtable, which draws on TPI research.
Figures labelled “2027 draft” refer to the draft budget now before Parliament. They are projections, not outcomes.
